scenario_user_message: So if my data changes every day, does that mean I should use RAG?

finalMessages.content: So if my data changes every day, does that mean I should use RAG?

content.text:
That's a good instinct, but you're actually reaching into a different node's territory. How often your data changes — data freshness — is covered by the sibling node "Data freshness dimension." That's where the "daily-changing data" question really belongs.

But since you're here, let me give you the cost angle on it, because it's the reason freshness matters so much economically.

The key cost fact: with fine-tuning, "keeping up with daily data" means re-training. Every time your data changes meaningfully, you pay the training cost again — compute, and the engineering time to build the pipeline that does it repeatedly. That's a recurring capital-ish cost.

With RAG, updating data is just updating your index or vector store — closer to a database write. That's cheap and incremental. You don't pay a big lump sum each time.

So from a pure cost-structure view: frequently-changing data pushes fine-tuning's cost up sharply because the expensive step (training) has to repeat, while RAG's expensive step (retrieval infrastructure) is a one-time-ish setup that absorbs updates cheaply.

But whether daily change actually *forces* RAG — that's the freshness node's call. Want me to stay on the cost mechanics, like what exactly makes up each side's cost?

With RAG, updating data is just updating the index or vector store, closer to a cheap incremental database write, so there's no big lump-sum cost each time data changes.

From a pure cost-structure view, frequently-changing data pushes fine-tuning's cost up sharply because its expensive step (training) must repeat, whereas RAG's expensive step (retrieval infrastructure) is a mostly one-time setup that absorbs updates cheaply.
